title: Bridging ambient- and high-pressure superconductivity in La$_2$LnNi$_2$O$_7$ films
authors: Motoki Osada, Chieko Terakura, Shusaku Imajo, Jean-Baptiste Morée, Akiko Kikkawa, Masamichi Nakajima, Hsiao-Yi Chen, Yusuke Nomura, Koichi Kindo, Ryotaro Arita, Yoshinori Tokura, Atsushi Tsukazaki
abstract: The discovery of high critical-temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ superconductivity near 80 K in bilayer nickelates under high pressure has sparked extensive studies. While superconductivity exceeding 40 K was subsequently discovered at ambient pressure in compressively strained films, the relationship between ambient- and high-pressure regimes remains an open question. Here we present a systematic investigation of superconductivity in compressively strained La$_2$LnNi$_2$O$_7$ films (Ln = lanthanides) at ambient and high pressures. The normal-state resistivity at ambient pressure, revealed by suppressing superconductivity with magnetic fields of 59 T, tends toward $T^2$ behaviour. Under high pressure in a cubic-anvil cell, $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ was enhanced from 41-42 K at ambient pressure to 67-73 K at 16 GPa. On the other hand, lattice compression induced by Ln substitution, which may mimic effects of pressure, lowers $T_{\mathrm{c}}$. In both cases, $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ correlates with the evolution of normal-state transport between $T^2$ and $T$-linear behaviour, offering insight into the interplay between lattice structure and superconductivity in bilayer nickelates.
summary: This study systematically investigates how superconductivity in nickelate films is affected by external pressure and chemical substitution. By combining high-pressure/high-field transport measurements with DFT calculations, the authors establish a strong correlation between lattice structure, orbital energy levels, and the enhancement of the superconducting critical temperature.
main_problem: The study aims to bridge the understanding of high-temperature superconductivity in bilayer nickelates ($	ext{La}_2	ext{LnNi}_2	ext{O}_7$) between ambient and high-pressure regimes.
main_result: Superconductivity is enhanced under high pressure (up to 73 K at 16 GPa), and both ambient and high-pressure $T_c$ correlate with the evolution of normal-state transport behavior ($ho \propto T^a$) and structural changes.
method: The research combines experimental measurements (resistivity under high magnetic fields and high pressure) with theoretical calculations using Density Functional Theory (DFT) to model the electronic structure.
model_or_system: The system is the bilayer nickelate $	ext{La}_2	ext{LnNi}_2	ext{O}_7$ film. The electronic structure is modeled using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian derived from Wannier orbitals spanning the $	ext{Ni}3d$ and $	ext{O}2p$ bands, focusing on the interplay between $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{3z^2-r^2}$ orbitals.
key_observables: Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), normal-state resistivity exponent ($a$), lattice parameters ($c/a$ ratio), and orbital energy differences ($\Delta E$).
important_parameters: High pressures (up to 20 GPa), high magnetic fields (up to 59 T), and the lanthanide element ($	ext{Ln}$) substitution.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that structural changes (pressure or substitution) directly modulate the electronic correlations governing superconductivity, as captured by the DFT model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural dependence of $T_c$ on lattice constants, the evolution of the normal-state resistivity exponent ($a$) with pressure, and DFT results showing band structures and Fermi surfaces under different compression levels.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates transport properties under extreme conditions (high P/B) and uses DFT to model the underlying electronic physics, correlating changes in orbital character and lattice structure to the superconducting transition temperature.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed, multi-faceted approach linking macroscopic transport measurements (P, B) to microscopic electronic structure calculations (DFT, Wannier orbitals), which is highly relevant for understanding correlated electron behavior in novel superconducting materials.
